issues.item: Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously
issues.explanation: The trigger set leans strongly toward direct combat/attack cues (suspicious people, gunshot noise), which is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of trauma to a loved one unless the loved one’s trauma specifically occurred in a combat or shooting context. As written, these triggers suggest personal threat exposure more than reminders of harm to a loved one.

The appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' implies prominent moral injury/self-blame for one’s own actions. That can occur after trauma to a loved one, but here there are no corresponding memory details or other appraisals linking the loved one’s trauma to the patient’s own actions/omissions. In this profile it pulls toward a different trauma meaning than the rest of the items and is not well supported by the selected trigger and memory content.

For trauma to a loved one, gunshot noise as a prominent trigger is hard to reconcile unless the loved one's trauma specifically involved gunfire. Nothing in the rest of the profile supports a gunfire/combat-linked bereavement context, so this trigger appears trauma-context mismatched.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' implies morally injurious personal action during the event. That is difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of trauma to a loved one unless there is additional context about the patient's own actions. The rest of the profile centers on loss, mistrust, and intrusive recall rather than perpetration-related guilt, making this item stand out as clinically incoherent.

vignette:
Linh Tran is a 29-year-old Vietnamese-American combat pilot, currently stationed at a domestic air base, who presented for psychological evaluation approximately fourteen months after witnessing the death of her younger brother during a family visit. Linh is single, lives alone in base housing, and was referred through the military's behavioral health service after a supervising officer noted a pattern of social withdrawal and what he described as "unusual rigidity" in her conduct over the preceding year.

Linh had taken emergency leave to visit her family in Houston following her brother Minh's diagnosis with a sudden cardiac condition. She was with him in the hospital room when he deteriorated rapidly during what was supposed to be a routine monitoring procedure. She held his hand as the code team worked, and she watched, from a chair pushed against the wall, as efforts to resuscitate him failed. What she could not stop seeing afterward - what returned to her with the quality of a photograph she had not chosen to take - was the precise angle of his face when the team stopped, the particular stillness of his chest, the way the monitor line went flat and stayed flat. These images did not fade with time. They returned in full resolution, uninvited, sometimes triggered by nothing she could name in advance: a certain quality of fluorescent light in a briefing room, the sound of a steady electronic tone during aircraft systems checks. In those moments the memory did not feel like remembering. It arrived whole, as though she were still in that room, and the present moment briefly ceased to exist around her.

In the months that followed, Linh constructed her life around the avoidance of anything that might bring her back to that hospital room. She stopped attending the informal gatherings that pilots on her base routinely used to decompress - not because she disliked her colleagues, but because conversations there moved unpredictably, and she had learned that any discussion touching on loss, on family, on someone else's grief, could pull the images forward without warning. She had begun to believe, with a certainty she could not argue herself out of, that she was fundamentally different from the people around her - that there was something broken in the architecture of who she was, something that had been there before Minh died and that his death had only revealed. She was certain that no one could be genuinely relied upon, that the appearance of support was provisional at best, and this conviction had quietly closed off the possibility of new connection. A colleague who had made several attempts to befriend her eventually stopped. Linh noticed, and felt neither surprise nor regret - only a flat confirmation of what she already believed.

She worked hard to keep Minh out of her conscious mind during flight operations, and she was largely successful in the cockpit, where procedural demands occupied her attention completely. But the effort of suppression was constant and exhausting in every other context. She avoided any colleague or family member who might raise the subject of what had happened, redirecting conversations with a practiced efficiency that had come to feel automatic. Her mother had called repeatedly in the early months; Linh had let most calls go unanswered. She had come to understand this not as cruelty but as self-preservation, though she was aware the distinction had cost her something in the relationship.

What finally brought her to seek help was a pre-mission briefing three weeks ago during which a fellow pilot mentioned, offhandedly, that his father had recently died. The memory of Minh's face returned so suddenly and so completely that Linh lost the thread of the briefing entirely and had to reconstruct it from notes afterward. She sat in the evaluation office describing this with a kind of controlled precision - the same tone she used for incident reports - and said that she could not afford for this to happen in the air. What she was most afraid of, though she did not say it in those words, was the appraisal she carried everywhere: that she had been present at the moment her brother needed protecting, and she had done nothing that mattered. What she was hoping for, tentatively and without much conviction, was some evidence that she was not as irreparably damaged as she had come to believe.
